query: I just graduated with $34,000 in student loans at 6.8% interest. Should I aggressively pay them off or start investing in my Roth IRA and 401k?
sources:
Source 1 (2023, NerdWallet, USA): Always capture the full employer 401k match first — it's an instant 50–100% return that beats any debt interest rate. After that, compare your loan rate to expected investment returns.

Source 2 (2022, Reddit r/PersonalFinance, USA): Community flowchart: capture employer match, pay off high-interest debt (above 6–7%), fund Roth IRA, then tackle lower-interest debt. At 6.8% you're right on the borderline.

Source 3 (2023, Investopedia, USA): Historically the S&P 500 returns ~10% annually before inflation, making investing instead of paying a 6.8% loan a positive expected value — but market downturns early in your career can make guaranteed debt payoff safer.

Source 4 (2022, Morningstar, USA): Roth IRA contributions in your 20s have decades to compound tax-free; delaying even five years can cost tens of thousands in retirement wealth, making the case for investing alongside debt repayment.

Source 5 (2023, WSJ, USA): Federal student loan income-driven repayment plans and potential forgiveness programs mean some borrowers are better off making minimum payments and maximizing investments, though recent policy uncertainty makes this risky.
atoms: geographic: USA federal student loan system
plausible_answers: Capture the full 401k match, fund a Roth IRA, then pay loan minimums, since market returns typically exceed 6.8%.
Pay off the loans fully before investing beyond the match, since a guaranteed 6.8% return is hard to beat risk-adjusted.
Enroll in income-driven repayment to minimize monthly payments and redirect cash into tax-advantaged accounts, betting on eventual forgiveness.
